title: An eye that sees (Avot 2:1)
hookLine: remember three things above you: an eye that sees, an ear that hears, a book that records
last: IT WILL BE WELL WITH YOU.

lines: THREE THINGS ON A STICKY NOTE.
cards: A police car slides into the rearview mirror, and suddenly the whole highway is driving the speed limit.
There's a similar gap between the person someone is in public and the person they are alone at eleven at night with a phone. Today's saying is about that gap.
It closes the teaching of Rabbi Judah the Prince we started yesterday: three things to keep in mind so you won't stumble. They're short enough for a sticky note on your fridge.

teach.h: AN EYE, AN EAR, A BOOK.
teach.b: Here's how he ends. Look at three things and you won't come into the grip of sin. Know what is above you: an eye that sees, an ear that hears, and all your deeds written in a book.

The first picture is being seen. The second is being heard, even the things you say under your breath, and that's the line we're carrying today. The third is being remembered: nothing you do simply vanishes.

The prophet Malachi has a picture like this, a book of remembrance written before God for the people who revere God and think about God's name. Now, this could sound like a security camera, something to make you nervous.
But it doesn't say an eye that punishes. It says an eye that sees.
The same eye sees the kindness nobody else noticed, the ear hears the quiet apology, and the book records yesterday's small good deed too. Being seen can be a comfort as much as a warning.
There's also a later reading, from Hasidic teachers, who played with the Hebrew words for know what is above you.

teach.h: WHAT IS ABOVE COMES FROM YOU.
teach.b: They read them as know that what is above comes from you: what happens up there depends on what you do down here.
Either way, the saying closes the gap between the public you and the eleven p.m. you. There's only one of you, and it's seen, heard, and remembered.

how: The saying is studied as a reminder that private conduct matters as much as public conduct, and that being seen includes the good as well as the bad.

games.why: know what is above you: an eye that sees, an ear that hears, and all your deeds written in a book.

practice: Imagine everything about this moment is noticed, not by a camera, but by someone who wishes you well: your posture, your breath, the worry you're carrying.

Let yourself be seen that way, then think of one thing you'll do today when nobody's watching, and picture doing it as if someone were. If you pray, you can remember that, in this teaching, God sees and hears.
